 Minister’s Message

                       Welcome to the 2026-2028 hunting and trapping seasons!

                       B.C.’s wildlife and the habitats that support them make this province unique and
                       special. From rugged coastlines and wind-swept grasslands to pristine lakes and
                       rivers, expansive forests and breathtaking alpine landscapes, B.C. offers endless
                       opportunities for every type of outdoor enthusiast.

                     Hunting in British Columbia supports sustainable food systems, contributes to
                     local economies, and funds conservation activities that benefits all who enjoy the
                     outdoors. Whether you are hiking trails, driving old roads or trekking through the
                     mountains, sustaining these opportunities requires a high level of care, responsibility
and diligence. For many, hunting is more than an activity—it is a tradition that connects families and
communities to the land, passing knowledge and respect for wildlife from one generation to the next.

As hunters, your willingness to contribute to conservation is making a difference in the Province. As a
specific example, your cooperation and partnership over the past 20 years in chronic wasting disease
(CWD) surveillance have been vital to monitoring and managing this threat. In 2024, the first cases of
CWD were detected in two deer in the Kootenay Region, and as of January 2026 there have been nine
confirmed cases.

We have increased monitoring and control efforts, including enhanced surveillance, targeted sampling,
public outreach and education, and special hunts; these efforts don’t work without the continued
participation and contributions of hunters. With your support, we can confirm prevalence remains below
1% in the affected areas. Through work with First Nations, hunters, local and federal governments and
non-government partners, we hope to keep prevalence low and reduce the risk of further spread.

In 2024, mandatory hunter reporting for moose and caribou was implemented. This has now been
expanded to include elk. The data submissions - for moose, caribou or elk that are due by March 31 of
each year – are providing useful and timely insights to help inform wildlife management decisions.

This synopsis, along with the associated Limited Entry Hunting Synopsis, includes numerous regulatory
changes since the 2024-26 hunting seasons. Please ensure you check for any possible in-season or
mid-cycle updates prior to hunting. There were also some proposed changes that were not made; the
proposed regulation to prohibit the use of lead shot for the purpose of hunting was put on hold, as were
some moose regulation changes in region 7b. We will do some more work to explore options to address
concerns raised through engagement. In the interim, please continue to reduce your use of lead shot to
avoid its accumulation in the environment.

To all British Columbians — whether you are hiking, camping, fishing, trapping, hunting or sharing
time outdoors with friends and family — I encourage you to enjoy all this province has to offer safely,
responsibly and with respect for the wildlife and habitats that sustain these opportunities. I wish you all
safe, memorable and successful 2026 and 2027 hunting seasons!

Finally, I would like to thank all staff in the wildlife program for your dedication to wildlife conservation
and health, sustainable management and responsible stewardship.

Randene Neill
Minister of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship

                                 Province-wide regulation changes for 2026-2028
    1. Mandatory Hunter Report required under all elk species licences.
    2. Incisor tooth no longer required for mountain sheep compulsory inspection.
    3. Possession and transport of cougar - evidence of sex must remain naturally attached to carcass.

    HOW CAN I HELP?
    1. Never confront a suspect.
    2. Record: suspect/vehicle information, type of violation, location, date and time.
    3. Report as soon as possible.
    The BC Wildlife Federation pays rewards up to $2000 for information leading to the charges of
    persons who have: violated laws related to the protection of fish, wildlife, or the environment; or
    damaged the property of companies or individuals who provide access to hunters and anglers.

     For violations related to tidal recreational fisheries and in-river salmon fisheries, contact Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) at 1-800-465-4336

                                                                         Buying Licences
» Licences are available online at www.gov.bc.ca/hunting and at Service BC, FrontCounter BC and participating commercial outlets and sporting
   goods stores. If you buy your species licence online, it will be mailed to you and it is subject to Canada Post delivery times. If you have not received
   your licences in the mail, you may qualify for a replacement free of charge if between 15 to 30 business days from the purchase date you report the
   loss to FrontCounter BC or Service BC.
» The following licences are electronic only and will be registered on your FWID profile after purchase: resident, non-resident or non-resident alien
   hunting licence, initiation licence, youth licence, upland game bird licence, Fraser Valley, and Gulf Islands special area licences. There is no
   requirement to carry a paper copy of these licence types while hunting.
» A parent or legal guardian must apply for the hunting or youth licence on behalf of the youth and sign the written undertaking that the parent or
   guardian will not allow the child or ward to hunt or carry firearms unless the youth is accompanied by and under the close personal supervision of a
   hunter who meets the prescribed qualifications to supervise.
» Hunters with permanent physical disabilities who are unable, because of their disability, to exit a vehicle to discharge a firearm, or are unable to walk
   100m while carrying a firearm, may apply for a disabled hunting permit. Information and the permit application process are available through the
   FrontCounter BC website at www.gov.bc.ca/disabled-hunting-permit.

Site and Access Restrictions                                                                                                                                                         9
                                                 Motor Vehicle Prohibitions and Restrictions
Detailed maps for all the Wildlife Act motor vehicle prohibitions in the province are now available online at www.gov.bc.ca/motorvehicleprohibitions.
There are 2 types of motor vehicle prohibitions under the Wildlife Act, and all types can be seasonal or year-round.
1. Motor Vehicle Closed Area: Prohibits the use or operation of a motor vehicle and e-bike. These prohibitions can be for all motor vehicles, or specific to
   ATVs/e-bikes or snowmobiles.
2. Motor Vehicle for Hunting Closed Area: The operation of motor vehicles and e-bikes to hunt, transport wildlife, transport equipment and supplies which
   are intended for or in support of hunting, or transport hunters to and from the location of wildlife is prohibited. These prohibitions can apply to all motor
   vehicles or be specific to ATVs/e-bikes or snowmobiles.
For definitions and regulations, see the Wildlife Act Motor Vehicle Prohibition Regulation. See regional sections for more details on Motor Vehicle Prohibitions.
Unless specifically exempted, all motor vehicle prohibitions include private land. Unless specifically included, motor vehicle prohibitions do not include highways
(as defined in the Motor Vehicle Act). See definitions section for vehicle types.
Information signs may be posted at the entry of closure areas. Where there are inconsistencies with signs and the regulation, the regulation is the final authority.

  Notice! Shot Ban
  The use of toxic (lead) shot for hunting waterfowl has been prohibited in British Columbia since 1995 and in Canada since 1997. The ban applies to all ducks,
  geese, coots and snipe. It does not apply to upland game birds (grouse, ptarmigan, quail, partridge, pheasants, and turkey), migratory upland game birds (pigeons,
  doves), ravens (where seasons exist), or target shooting, although a local restriction may be implemented if there is a conflict with an important wetland.
  Federal regulations currently identify steel shot, bismuth shot, tungsten-iron shot, tungsten-bronze-iron shot, tin shot, tungsten - matrix shot, and tungsten-polymer
  shot as the only non-toxic shot permitted for use on waterfowl, coot, and snipe. Hunters are advised to contact the CWS Canadian Wildlife Service in Delta (604-
  350-1950) for more details.

Legal Hunting Methods and Provincial Bag Limits                                                                                                                            13
                                                                           Deer Bag Limits
     One of the most common questions that wildlife staff receive is about deer bag limits and deer species licences. On the surface it seems confusing,
     with provincial bag limits vs. regional bag limits, buck limits vs. antlerless bag limits, aggregate bag limits, individual bag limits for species, and species
     licences for mule (black-tailed) and white-tailed deer. Once the system is broken down into its parts it is straight forward.
     There are two classes of bag limits, Provincial and Regional, neither of these bag limits can be exceeded.
     1.    The provincial bag limit for deer is 3 (not including Haida Gwaii). Hunters may not harvest more than 3 deer in one licence year, only 1 may be a
            mule (black-tailed) deer buck from regions 3, 4, 5, 6, 7A, 7B, and 8 combined. Hunters may harvest 3 white-tailed deer (if they purchase 3 white-
            tailed deer licences), or 3 mule (black-tailed) deer (if they purchase 3 mule (black-tailed) deer licences), or a combination of white-tailed and mule
            (black-tailed) deer (1+2 or 2+1) providing they do not exceed the provincial limit of 3 and not more than 1 mule (black-tailed) deer buck from
            regions 3, 4, 5, 6 ,7A, 7B, and 8 combined. The reason hunters may purchase more than 3 deer licences in total is to provide hunters with the
            flexibility to harvest any combination of white-tailed or mule (black-tailed) deer up to a maximum of 3.
     2. Regional bag limits are implemented to limit the number of a species or sex of deer that may be harvested per hunter per year in response to local
           conditions. If a hunter harvests the maximum number of a species or sex of deer within a region, they can no longer hunt deer of the same species
           and sex within that region. They can, however, continue to hunt and harvest deer in other regions until they reach the provincial bag limit of 3.
     The following table outlines the provincial and regional bag limits for deer. Deer bag limits on Haida Gwaii are not covered in this article, as they are a unique
     case.

After Your Hunt                                                                                                                                                                  17
     How to Extract an Incisor Tooth from your Sheep, Moose, Caribou or other Ungulates
     Incisor teeth only occur at the front of the lower jaw of an ungulate, their removal is easy and will not
     affect your opportunity to have the animal taxidermy mounted. It is important that a middle tooth is                     Front Incisor Teeth
     removed from the jaw properly, so that the animal can be aged. Your assistance in taking care to properly
     remove an incisor tooth from the jaw, clean it and submit it is an important part of this process.
                                                                                                                                 Crown
     Extracting the teeth                                                                                                   I2       I1        I1
     Incisor teeth can be easily extracted from the freshly killed hoofed animal or ungulate; their
                                                                                                                                                       I2
     removal becomes much more difficult if the jaw has been dried. You may need to soak the jaw in
     warm water to rehydrate it, making removal easier. To remove a tooth:
     To remove a tooth:                                                                                                      Cut
     1. Cut down through the gum tissue on either side of the root with a thin-bladed sharp knife. Select one               along                   Root
         of the center teeth, as they have the largest developed root and will give the most accurate estimate               dashed
         of age.                                                                                                             lines
     2. Push the tooth out with your thumb. If the tooth does not come out easily, carefully use a pair of
         pliers and pull it out with a twisting motion. Clean off the soft tissue and any jawbone material from
         the tooth. Do not cut into the root or submit a tooth with a broken root as it is the root portion of the tooth that is used in aging.
     IMPORTANT
     •      Do not send the entire jawbones.
     •      Do not include soft tissue (gum tissues, muscle, hide) with the tooth.
     •      Do not store your tooth in a plastic bag. Place the cleaned tooth inside a paper envelope to dry.
     •      Ensure the envelope is labelled with species, date of kill, region, management unit, FWID and which tooth is being submitted (I1, I2).

                                                                      Ungulate Health
 Concerns with ungulate health are rising with the recent detection of Adenovirus Hemorrhagic Disease (AHD) in B.C. and detection of Chronic Wasting
 Disease (CWD) within the southeast part of the Kootenay Region. AHD was first identified in the fall of 2020 on several Gulf Islands (Galiano, Mayne,
 Pender, and Salt Spring) and southern Vancouver Island as far north as Merville. AHD is a highly contagious and often fatal disease, particularly in
 black-tailed deer. It has caused significant losses of deer in the U.S.
 The disease course is usually rapid as the virus damages small blood vessels in the lungs and intestines. Symptoms of AHD include difficulty
 breathing, foaming, or drooling from the mouth, diarrhea, and seizures. If an infected animal survives the acute phase, chronic signs may include ulcers
 and abscesses in the mouth and throat that can lead to weight loss and death. Fawns/juveniles are more susceptible to AHD and experience much
 higher death rates than adults. Affected animals are often found dead and in good body condition with no signs of trauma or other cause of death.
 AHD can be spread through direct contact between deer or contact with fluids (saliva, feces, urine). Transmission may also occur through airborne
 routes, contaminated feed and water, and contaminated equipment. There is no evidence that AHD can be transmitted to humans and research
 supports that it is not transmitted to livestock or pets. Although there is no known risk to human health from AHD, hunters are advised not to consume
 meat from animals found dead, obviously ill or acting abnormally prior to death. To help prevent the spread of AHD, dispose of carcasses by deep
 burial, do not move infected, dead or live deer to new areas, and prevent aggregations of deer at artificial feeding or water sources.
 CWD has been detected in B.C. and the risk of further spread continues to increase as high-risk material is moved around the province or brought into
 the B.C. Natural movement of infected animals puts certain parts of B.C. at greatest risk, but the disease could be introduced anywhere, including
 Vancouver Island, with the transport of infected carcasses and use of CWD contaminated material (i.e., urine-based scents). Help protect B.C.
 ungulates by understanding these risks, helping to increase awareness, and submitting your deer, elk, moose or caribou for testing. Learn more about
 the BC CWD Program at www.gov.bc.ca/chronicwastingdisease and AHD at www.gov.bc.ca/wildlifehealth.

The Kootenay Region offers a diversity of wildlife and habitats and significant opportunities to enjoy the outdoors. Every person should have a stewardship mindset
to take care of the impact they may have on the living and non-living components. Biologists have a few important reminders for hunters in the Kootenay Region:
  • Chronic Wasting Disease was confirmed in white-tailed deer and mule deer populations in the Kootenay Region in January 2024.
  • An emergency response has been initiated to prevent spread and access samples to better understand the extent of the outbreak.
  • A high risk boundary (the CWD Management Zone) that includes MUs 4-1 to 4-8 and 4-20 to 4-25 has been defined based on animal movement and proximity to
     CWD cases in BC, Alberta and Montana.
  • Mandatory testing is expanded to include deer, elk and moose harvested within the CWD Management Zone and samples must be submitted to a designated
     freezer before leaving this area. For freezer locations see www.gov.bc.ca/CWDdropoff
  • There is a 24-hour exemption after harvest on specified routes for deer, elk or moose harvested in M.U. 4-7, M.U. 4-8, and M.U. 4-25 that require travel outside
     of the CWD Management Zone to immediately access a designated CWD freezer. See page 15 for specific routes.
  • Brain tissue and spinal column (except for the tail) from deer, elk and moose harvested within the CWD Management Zone cannot be transport outside of this
     boundary. It is recommended to leave these parts at or near the kill site or dispose of them at a landfill before leaving the area.
  • We encourage hunters to continue hunting in the affected areas; hunting can help to suppress transmission and spread by removing infected animals from the
     landscape. It is estimated that less than 1% of cervids currently have CWD in these areas.
  • Hunting is the most important tool for managing CWD as it helps to suppress disease prevalence and provides essential information to support science-based
     management of CWD.
  • For more information visit: www.gov.bc.ca/chronicwastingdisease

44                                                                                                                                2026–2028 Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis
 Region 5 – Cariboo
 Notice to hunters:
 The Cariboo Region overlaps the Traditional Territories of the four member nations of the Northern Secwepemc te Qelmucw (Xatśūll Cmetem’ (Soda Creek)),
 Stswēcem'c Xgāt’tem (Canoe/Dog Creek), T’ēxelc (Williams Lake First Nation) and Tsq’ēsceń (Canim Band), and independent Secwepemc communities:
 Esk’etemc, High Bar, Whispering Pines/Clinton Indian Band; the six member nations of the Tsilhqot’in Nation (Tl’etinqox, Tl’esqox, ʔEsdilagh, Tŝideldel, Xeni
 Gwet’in and Yuneŝit’in), Ulkatcho First Nation, three member nations of the Southern Dakelh Nation Alliance (Lhoosk’uz Dene, Lhtako Dene and Nazko First
 Nation), Nuxalk, Wuikinuxv, Gitga’at, Heiltsuk, Gwa’Sala-‘Nakwaxda’xw, Xwémalhkwu (Homalco), and Nanwakolas Council member nation Da’naxda’xw/
 Awaetlala.
 Members of these First Nations exercise their aboriginal rights to hunt, fish, and trap throughout their territory in the region and hunters are asked to be
 respectful of these traditional practices. Culturally sensitive areas are located throughout the Cariboo and hunters are asked to minimize their impacts to
 the land through responsible hunting and camping practices and packing out what is packed in. Indigenous Nations monitor activities within their traditional
 territories and may connect with hunters to share information and foster positive relations between resident hunters and indigenous communities.
 If you are interested in learning more about Indigenous traditional values and stewardship practices, hunters may contact local First Nation offices directly.
 Notice to hunters - Report feral pigs
 In B.C., feral pigs are previously domesticated pigs, or their descendants, and have been reported in low numbers in parts of the province, including in the
 Cariboo Region. Feral pigs are destructive to crops and private property. They can prey upon livestock such as goats and sheep and can spread diseases and
 parasites to people, livestock, and wildlife. Feral pigs can also affect ecosystem processes from the soil up, by extensive digging and their wallows can affect
 pond and wetland structure. They also compete with native wildlife for food, as well as feed on reptiles, eggs of ground nesting birds, and small mammals.
 Please report feral pig sightings in the Cariboo Region via the webform available on the B.C. Inter-Ministry Invasive Species Working Group website: www.gov.
 bc.ca/invasive-species.

 Notice to hunters – Report elk sightings
 Historically elk ranged across much of the grasslands and forests of the Cariboo Region and were a critical species supporting predator-prey systems and were
 highly valued by First Nations for traditional uses. Elk are becoming more numerous and increasing their range in the Cariboo-Chilcotin, with increased reports
 of sightings and increased counts during population inventories.
 The Cariboo Region is currently undertaking elk management planning and reports of elk observations will support this process. Please report Elk sightings to
 the FrontCounter BC Williams Lake Office at (250) 398-4574.

 Notice to hunters!
 The traditional territories of 34 First Nations have existed for time immemorial in this area prior to the creation of Wildlife Management Units
 and licensed hunting. Hunters are encouraged to learn about the history and culture of the First Nation(s) and their traditional territories that
 you’ll be hunting on. Please respect the land by leaving your campsites clean and free of garbage and avoid using traditional camp sites and
 cabins. If you encounter Indigenous land guardians during your travels treat them with respect as they fulfill their duties as stewards of the
 land and our partners in resource stewardship. www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/environment/natural-resource-stewardship/consulting-with-
 first-nations/first-nations-negotiations/first-nations-a-z-listing
 » The Nisga’a Government wishes to urge hunters to use caution when hunting in the Nass Valley, because there may be a large number of people
  picking mushrooms during the hunting season.
 » Lake Babine Nation (LBN) is requesting the assistance of hunters to ensure that all parts of wildlife harvested within their traditional territory (MU
  6-5, 6-6, 6-7, and 6-8) are utilized. LBN requests that hunters phone the Natural Resource Office at (250)-692-4780 to coordinate drop-off of any
  portions of carcasses they are willing to share or would otherwise leave in the field (e.g., heads, hide, heart, and kidneys) and encourages BC hunters
  to contact them prior to beginning a trip. For further information on meat sharing and other initiatives, please find contact info at www.lakebabine.
  com/.
 » The Teslin Tlingit Council (TTC) is requesting the assistance of hunters to ensure that all parts of wildlife harvested within the Teslin Tlingit
  Traditional Territory in northern BC (MU 6-25) are used. TTC requests that hunters contact TTC Game Guardians (867-390-2532 ext. 377 or 373) to
  arrange for sharing portions of any wildlife harvest that would otherwise be left in the field (e.g., heads). Game Guardians are active in the Traditional
  Territory, educating the public and promoting safe and respectful hunting. TTC encourages BC hunters to contact the Lands and Resources office
  prior to beginning your trip.
 » The Kaska Nation are requesting the assistance of hunters to ensure that all parts of wildlife harvested within their traditional territories in
  northern British Columbia (MU 6-23, 6-24, and 6-25) are utilized. The Kaska Nation request that hunters drop off any portions of carcasses they
  would otherwise leave in the field (e.g., heads) or are willing to share. For further information on culturally sensitive areas, meat sharing, and other
  initiatives, please find contact info for the Kaska Nation at: www.kaskadenacouncil.com
 »The Gitxsan Simgigyet (Hereditary Chiefs) and their Wilp (members) manage their Laxyip (Traditional Lands). You may encounter Gitxsan Laxyip
  Management Guardians monitoring conditions and activities within the Laxyip, on behalf of their Simgigyet and Wilp. Wildlife Management Units
  6-7, 6-8, 6-9, 6-15, 6-17, 6-18, 6-30, 7-27, and 7-39 overlap the Gitxsan Laxyip. Hunters are encouraged to respect the land and wildlife and minimize
  impacts to the land through responsible hunting and camping practices which follows the Gitxsan Ayookw (Traditional Laws) to ensure that the
  Laxyip remains healthy for future generations. For further information, including maps and meat sharing opportunities, please contact the Gitxsan
  Laxyip Management Office at 250-842-0755.

     Notice to hunters!
     McLeod Lake Indian Band asks hunters to respect their Treaty Settlement Lands. Access to these lands require permission from the local Band Office and it is the
     hunter’s responsibility to be aware of these Treaty Settlement Lands/ Indian Reserves. For more information visit www.mlib.ca/departments/land-stewardship/
     hunter-information/.
     For persons hunting in MUs 7-29 (north of Nation River), 7-37 or 7-38 you will be within the traditional territory of the Tsay Keh Dene Nation (TKDN). For persons
     hunting in MUs 7-39 to 7-41 you will be within either the traditional territory of the Kwadacha or Tsay Keh Dene Nation depending on your location. Before you
     hunt, please check at the appropriate Nation’s office, by phone or email, to receive important information pertinent to safety and environmental concerns.
     TKDN offers a voluntary Licensed Hunter Registration System for those hunting in TKDN territory. This system informs the Nation of hunting and harvest
     statistics while providing a safety and communication resource for hunters. If you have any questions or concerns, please contact the department of Lands and
     Resources at fw.coordinator@tkdb.ca or (250) 562-8882. www.tsaykeh.com/departments/lrto/
     If you will be hunting in Kwadacha Nation’s traditional territory, it is strongly encouraged that you contact the Lands and Resources Officer (LRO) in Kwadacha at
     (250) 471-2302 or email lands@kwadacha.com. We ask that you visit www.kwadacha.com website and fill out both the Notification to Hunt and Hunter Harvest
     Surveys and submit to the LRO, so that safety and open communication between hunters and the Dane Nan Yḗ Dāh Land Guardians is established.
     Nak’azdli Whut’en is requesting the assistance of hunters to ensure that all parts of wildlife harvested within the Nak’azdli Whut’en Traditional Territory are
     used. Nak’azdli Whut’en requests that hunters contact the Land Guardians (250-996-0088) to arrange for sharing portions of any wildlife harvest that would
     otherwise be left in the field (e.g., hides, organs) in MUs 7-13 to 7-15, 7-24 to 7-26, 7-28, 7-29, and 7-38. Nak’azdli Whut’en also encourages hunters to contact
     the Yinka Huwunline office prior to beginning your trip in these MUs.


                                               Wildlife Management Update from the Omineca Region
 Results from population monitoring since 2020 suggest that moose numbers have stabilized in the southern and central parts of the region
 and have slightly increased west of Prince George. While the recent trends are positive, numbers are still well below densities observed in the
 early 2000s. Research on the factors influencing moose population dynamics continues (www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/environment/plants-
 animals-ecosystems/wildlife/wildlife-conservation/moose/moose-conservation/moose-research) and moose habitat work has provided
 moose-friendly approaches to forest harvesting, including Ungulate Winter Ranges (UWRs) for moose where forest harvesting is paired with
 management requirements to maintain or improve moose habitat. Inventory work continues for elk, mule deer, thinhorn sheep, mountain
 goat, caribou, grizzly bear, wolf, lynx, fisher, and marten. Collaborations among Ministry biologists, First Nations, and stakeholders are further
 investigating limiting factors and monitoring approaches for mountain goats, elk, and thinhorn sheep in the region. Harvesting a collared
 animal is not illegal if taken lawfully. If you harvest a collared animal, please report it to the RAPP line to confirm whether the animal is safe
 to eat due to the possible presence of wildlife immobilization drugs in the meat and return the collar to the Conservation Officer Service or
 any Ministry office. BC strives to maintain the health of wildlife populations in collaboration with our partners for the benefit of all British
 Columbians. Our goals are to ensure that Indigenous hunters can exercise their right to hunt within their Traditional Territories and to promote
 licensed hunter and trapper opportunities, including resident experience and a sustainable guide-outfitter industry.

   Notice to hunters!
   Treaty 8 is the foundation of the relationship between Treaty 8 First Nations, the Crown, and all people present in Treaty 8 territory.
   Treaty 8 First Nations exercise their treaty rights to hunt, fish, and trap throughout the region and ask that hunters be respectful of
   others on the land base and of treaty rights, culturally sensitive areas and treaty settlement lands. You may encounter Indigenous
   Guardians monitoring conditions and activities on the land. Respectful dialogue with the Guardians and Treaty 8 members is welcome
   and encouraged

   Dane nan yḗ dāh Kaska Land guardians are actively monitoring and patrolling in the Kaska traditional territory, interacting and sharing
   information with all land users in regards to promoting safe and respectful hunting. Daylu Dena Council encourages B.C. hunters to
   contact the Daylu Lands and Resources (located in Lower Post) office at 250-779-3161 Ext. 0 and Dease River First Nation Lands and
   Resources officer (located in Good Hope Lake) at 250-239-3646 prior to beginning your trip.

Trapping Regulations                                                                                                                                                           71
                                                            Online Licensed Trapping Harvest Report
     The Ministry of Water, Land, and Resource Stewardship has introduced the online Trapping Harvest Report. Licensed trappers must submit a trapping harvest
     report each trapping licence year (July 1 to June 30). The report is due 31 days after the end of the licence year (by July 31). A trapper can submit one report
     at the end of the year, or multiple reports throughout the year. All trapping activity must be reported by July 31 following the end of the trapping licence year.
     A report is required even if no harvest occurred.
     Licensed trappers who do not submit all their trapping activity by July 31 following the licence year will not be able purchase a licence, permit, limited entry
     hunting application or guide territory certificates under the Wildlife Act until a report is submitted. Licensed trappers may also be charged with a $460 fine if a
     report is not submitted by the deadline.
     Trappers can submit their report online through the WILD system, or by submitting a completed report form (available online) to any FrontCounter BC office.
     Information required on the report includes:
      • Trapper’s Fish and Wildlife ID (FWID)       • Management Unit                        • Month
      • Trapping licence number                     • Species                                • Park name and Park Use Permit, if applicable
      • Trapline number or private property         • Sex and quantity harvested
     Additional information on how to submit a report is available on the Trapping in BC website www.gov.bc.ca/trapping-reporting.
     Compulsory Reporting and Compulsory Inspection of furbearers is still required.
     Permit holders do not report their permit trapping activities in the Trapping Harvest Report. Permit holders will continue to report as required under their
     permit.
     Individuals who are exempt from holding a trapping licence in B.C. are not required to report but a voluntary reporting option is provided.

                                                    Hunting and Trapping Ethics
It is extremely important for hunters and trappers to realize that they use a public resource! With this privilege it is vital to maintain a perception among the public that
we hunt and trap in an ethical and humane manner. The majority of British Columbians support hunting and trapping to one degree or another, but there is a prevalent
misunderstanding among the general public as to the role that hunters and trappers play in conservation and environmental stewardship. Fueling that misunderstand-
ing are images and media reports of hunters and trappers who are at least perceived to be acting in a less than upstanding manner, or who disrespect the wildlife they
pursue.
It is important for all of us to remember not only the legal obligations, but also the unwritten rules of ethics that keep hunting a great sport.
• Safety for yourself, your companions, and the public is the most important aspect of hunter training. Hunting accidents continue to be very rare because we all know
  that there is no room for recklessness at the expense of safety and courtesy.
• Have respect for the sensitivities of others. Do not display your kill or firearms where it may offend other people. What may impress your friends may not have the
  same effect on your neighbours.
• Respect wildlife and the sanctity of the harvested animals’ lives. Strive to make every kill a clean one. Prepare your firearm in advance of, and during, the season to
  ensure accuracy and dependability. Practice your marksmanship at a licensed firing range, and do not shoot unless you have a clear shot of a vital part of the animal.
  Remember: “you can’t pull the bullet back.”
• Prepare the meat properly. Proper handling of meat is easy to learn and to not do so is both illegal and wasteful.
• Respect the environment by packing out everything you pack in! Nobody wants to arrive at a campsite and clean up the mess left by the previous occupants.
• Do not consume drugs or alcohol while hunting or trapping.
• Respect private property. Always seek permission from landowners and thank them for the opportunities given. Unless explicitly stated, permission granted once
  does not entitle you to access the property on subsequent occasions.
• Please respect gates, fences, and equipment as they are there for a reason. Leave everything the way you found it.
• Be the eyes and ears for the enforcement agencies and report those who break the law. Remember the RAPP program 1-877-952-7277 (RAPP) or rapp.bc.ca.
• Be aware that you are a mentor when youth are observing.
• Respect your fellow hunters. Work with one another to promote good relationships, safety, knowledge and a fair distribution of opportunity and harvest
• Lead by example, you are an ambassador for the public and media image of hunting.


Ethical hunters and trappers are critical to effective and sustainable wildlife management, and to the ethical hunter we offer our sincerest gratitude. Opportunities for
the sustainable use of wildlife are possible because of you.

Important Notice for Mountain Goat Hunters
Regulations are in place to minimize female (nanny) mountain goat harvest, or on Blunt
Mountain (MU 6-8) during the bow only season to prohibit nanny harvest, as an important
conservation action. Outreach has consistently encouraged hunters to select a male
(billy) mountain goat, when making a decision to harvest. The B.C. regulation states:
“It is unlawful to hunt a female mountain goat accompanying a kid or a female mountain
goat in a group that contains one or more kids.”
This regulation does not protect all female mountain goats as a solitary female mountain
goat, or a female mountain goat within a group of goats that does not contain kids, would
still be legal to harvest. That said, recent analysis of harvest demographic data since
2012 suggests that the proportion of females in the harvest has generally decreased;
still in some localized areas, there continues to be concerns over the high proportions of
female mountain goats in the harvest.
For more information on how to distinguish between a billy and a nanny visit m.youtube.
com/watch?v=J8gUaMx8G7I, after watching the video test yourself on mountain goat sex
identification at www.adfg.alaska.gov/index.cfm?adfg=quiz.mountaingoatquiz.
You can also find additional information on the websites of the BC Mountain Goat Society
(www.bcmountaingoatsociety.ca/), and the Rocky Mountain Goat Alliance (goatalliance.
org/).

 Respiratory Disease in Wild Sheep and Mountain Goats
 Disease introduction has contributed to declines in bighorn sheep populations across their range. Wild sheep and mountain goats are susceptible to
 a variety of infectious organisms carried by domestic sheep and goats. Of particular importance are bacteria that cause respiratory diseases such
 as pneumonia including specific strains of Pasteurella multocida, Mannheimia haemolytica and Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae. These bacteria are
 often carried by domestic sheep and goats where they may or may not cause disease. In contrast, when wild sheep and goats are exposed to these
 bacteria, they do not develop an effective immune response and pneumonia outbreaks can occur which may result in die-offs, affecting 5-95% of the
 herd. Following an outbreak the disease may also persist in survivors, resulting in kid mortalities and many years of low lamb survival, followed by
 population declines. Research efforts have confirmed that physical separation of wild and domestic sheep and goats is the only management tool
 currently available to reduce the risk of disease transmission.

 To assist in maintaining this separation, producers of domestic sheep and goats on private land located in areas shared by wild sheep or in close
 proximity to mountain goats are encouraged to better understand this issue and to work with wildlife managers to reduce risk of transmission, see:

     • https://wafwa.org/wpdm-package/2025-recommendations-for-domestic-sheep-and-goat-management-in-wild-sheep-habitat/
     • www. gov.bc.ca/wildlife-health/wild-sheep-health
     • www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/industry/agriculture-seafood/animals-and-crops/animal-production/sheep-and-goats/mycoplasma-ovipneumoniae

 If you observe wild sheep or mountain goats displaying potential signs of poor health (i.e., excessive coughing, running noses, diarrhea, lethargy or
 scabbing around the eyes, nose, and mouth), or wild sheep or goats in the same pasture as domestic sheep and goats, please report it to the RAPP
 line at 1-877-952-7277, or the local Ministry Regional Office.
 For more information on wild sheep and diseases, please see the documents and webpages developed by the Western Association of Fish
 and Wildlife Agencies (www.wafwa.org), the Wild Sheep Foundation (www.wildsheepfoundation.org) and the Wild Sheep Society of BC (www.
 wildsheepsociety.com). Further, see the Wild Sheep Society of BC’s article in this synopsis on the collaborative BC Sheep Separation Program.




 Wild Sheep Genetics

 Wild sheep species distributions as well as their habitats in North America, have been shaped by repeated, historical glaciation events that created
 significant barriers to gene flow, resulting in our present-day distributions of Thinhorn and Bighorn sheep.
 There are two subspecies of Thinhorn sheep, that have traditionally been classified based on pelage colour: the white coated and more northerly
 distributed Dall’s sheep, and the dark coated and more southerly distributed Stone’s sheep. While this system of classification works across the majority
 of thinhorn sheep range, sheep with a wide range of dark and intermediate colouration occur in south-central Yukon and north-western British Columbia.
 These sheep are commonly referred to as Fannin sheep and some consider them to be Stone’s sheep, because of their non-white pelage.
 Over the past two decades, researchers have used genetic analyses to improve our knowledge of Thinhorn sheep genetic relationships, also informing our
 understanding of Dall’s, Stone’s and Fannin sheep range distributions. This research has shown that previous geographic and colour-based subspecies
 classifications are not accurate. Recent work led from BC and in partnership with other jurisdictions and the University of Alberta was able to show that
 nearly the entire global population of Stone’s sheep resides in BC, and that Fannin sheep (once thought to be Stone’s sheep), found in south-central Yukon
 and north-western BC, are genetically more closely related to Dall’s sheep than Stone’s.


 Wild and Domestic Sheep Contact
 Across North America wild sheep herds have suffered catastrophic all-age die-offs, compounded by high lamb mortality and slow population recovery
 periods, from respiratory disease (pneumonia) transmitted from domestic sheep and goats. Despite several attempts, no
 vaccination, treatments or preventative measures, other than physical separation, have been found to be broadly successful
 at preventing exposure to Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae (M. ovi); the bacteria most responsible for most respiratory disease
 outbreaks in wild sheep. In a number of jurisdictions, test-and remove programs (where wild sheep are captured, health                                  Photo: Lino Grifone
 sampled and those that are infected with M.ovi, are removed) have been evaluated as a potential method to manage
 respiratory disease in affected wildlife sheep herds. Building from this learning,, from disease management initiative tested
 in other jurisdictions, B.C. along with support from NGOs and First Nations communities, has initiated similar test-and-remove
 projects in provincial bighorn sheep herds that have continued to struggle with respiratory disease. Ongoing monitoring has
 demonstrated significant improvement in lamb survival following removal of infected herd mates.
 B.C. continues to use many approaches to enhance wild sheep protections and restorie wild sheep populations. With funding
 from the Habitat Conservation Trust Foundation, Ministry of Agriculture and Food, Wild Sheep Foundation, the Wild Sheep
 Society of BC and support from the Province, the BC Sheep Separation Program is working to test domestic sheep and goats
 for M. ovi in high risk of contact areas near wild sheep range, and to promote education and outreach to domestic sheep and
 goat farmers to reduce the risk of contact and disease transmission between domestic and wild sheep and goats. In support
 of these initiatives, the Province continues to offer information on our websites:
     • www.gov.bc.ca/wildlife-health/wild-sheep-health
     • www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/industry/agriculture-seafood/animals-and-crops/animal-production/sheep-and-goats/mycoplasma-ovipneumoniae

 To report any interactions between wild sheep and domestic sheep or goats call the RAPP Line 1-877-952-7277.

                                                                                                                                                   79
                                               Southern Mountain and Boreal Caribou Update
     Woodland caribou have roamed British Columbia (B.C.) for thousands of years. They are a nationally recognized icon, contributing to the beauty and
     biodiversity of our province and nation. Unfortunately, the number of caribou in B.C. declined steadily over past decades, dropping from about 40,000
     to approximately 17,000 animals. Southern Mountain and Boreal caribou populations are currently listed as “Threatened” under the Federal Species at
     Risk Act, and significant efforts are underway to support the protection and recovery of these herds. Recent recovery efforts are helping stabilize and
     increase some caribou herds, with the population now around 19,000 across B.C.
     The reasons for caribou population declines are complex, with multiple interacting factors (e.g., habitat change, predation, natural disturbance, climate
     change, etc.) and may differ somewhat across the province. In most cases, however, caribou population declines are driven by predator-prey imbalances
     resulting from habitat change that have led to unsustainable rates of predation towards caribou. Not surprisingly, evidence collected through research
     and monitoring in B.C. suggests the best results for caribou recovery are achieved when multiple recovery actions are taken (i.e., combinations of
     habitat protection and restoration, predator reduction, maternal penning, supplemental feeding, etc.). Long-term success for caribou recovery will
     depend on landscape-level habitat protection and restoration, however, it may be decades before the benefits of such measures are realized. It will be a
     combination of population recovery actions that provide immediate benefits along with long-term habitat protection and restoration initiatives that will
     help achieve the overarching objective self-sustaining caribou herds.
     The Province continues to use a comprehensive and adaptive approach to conservation that is informed by science and traditional knowledge.
     Caribou recovery initiatives currently underway include:
     • .Together with our partners, the Province is advancing recovery planning and implementation for many caribou herds across the province.
     • Predator reduction efforts implemented to support caribou recovery are applied to select herds across B.C. and have contributed to stabilizing or
       increasing population trends in many of those herds.
     • Indirect reduction of wolf populations by stabilizing moose populations through increased hunting opportunities, which is being applied in one
       caribou range. However, moose enhancement objectives exist in many areas outside of caribou range.
     • Maternity pens to protect female caribou and their newborn calves from predators are in place in northern and southern BC.
     • Supplemental feeding trials to support nutritional intake are in place in select herds.
     • Population monitoring and enhanced research on caribou habitat use, mortality causes, and survival rates through the use of satellite GPS collar
       technology.
     • A number of habitat restoration projects are underway, including ground lichen seeding and restoration of linear features.
     • Habitat protection measures, including the establishment of new Ungulate Winter Ranges, Wildlife Habitat Areas, and expansion of Provincial Parks.
     • Motorized recreation restrictions and closures to reduce potential disturbance and displacement of caribou.

     What should you know as an outdoor recreation enthusiast?
     If you are lucky enough to see caribou, shut off any recreational all-terrain vehicles and let the caribou pass. Snow machines, helicopters, or skiers
     may increase stress on caribou, which can reduce their energy reserves during winter and affect over-winter survival and/or reproductive success the
     following summer. Continued disturbance can also result in range abandonment by caribou. Your support of recreational closures will contribute to
     caribou recovery.
     Of note, Northern Mountain caribou are listed under the Federal Species at Risk Act as “Special Concern”, meaning they are not facing many of the
     same challenges that Southern Mountain and Boreal caribou are facing. Many Northern Mountain caribou herds are abundant and self-sustaining and
     can support licensed hunting opportunities.
     More information on caribou recovery in B.C. can be obtained at gov.bc.ca/caribou


                                                              Notice to Black Bear Hunters
     In order to ensure the sustainability of bear hunting, bear hunters are requested to:
     1. Be patient. Don’t shoot the moment you see a bear!
     2. Observe carefully and select an adult, male bear. Bears can look deceptively large. Adult males have larger home ranges and will tend to be encountered less
         frequently than females and younger males.
     3. Be aware that there is no open season on any bear less than two years old or any bear in its company (i.e., the sow). Take the time to ensure that cubs are
         not nearby.
     4. Be aware there is no open season on grizzly bear or white (Kermode) or blue (Glacier) colour phases of the black bear.
     5. Contact the nearest Fish and Wildlife office immediately for important information if you shoot an ear-tagged or radio-collared bear. See Ear Tags and Collars
         section, page 11.

                                             Wildlife Health

Wildlife Health
Wildlife health is closely linked to environmental, domestic animal, and human health. Assessment of
wildlife health benefits everyone. Your observations about how wild animals appear and behave can
provide information on B.C. wildlife population health and sustainability. Videos, photos, and written/verbal
descriptions may be valuable. For more information on/contacts for wildlife health see: www.gov.bc.ca/
wildlifehealth or the Canadian Wildlife Health Cooperative website at: www.cwhc-rcsf.ca.

Human Health
For threats to human health, (e.g., West Nile virus, parasites, and Lyme’s disease), pick up a copy of
Diseases You Can Get from Wildlife from a government office or visit: www.gov.bc.ca/wildlifehealth. For
more information on specific diseases see: BC Centre for Disease Control website: www.bccdc.ca/health-
info. Note information on the recently recognized parasite, Echinococcus multilocularis.

Chronic Wasting Disease
Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) is a fatal neurological disease                       STOP CHRONIC
found in species of the deer family (cervids). Infected animals may                 WASTING DISEASE
not appear sick as signs take months to develop after infection. In                 Do Not Import
advanced stages of the disease, weight loss, behaviour changes,                     Intact Deer Carcasses
drooling, poor coordination, and trembling may be seen. If you                      Keep B.C. Wildlife Healthy
observe a cervid with these symptoms please report them and their
location to the Conservation Officer Service through the RAPP Line
(1-877-952-7277) or to the B.C. Wildlife Health Program at CWD@gov.bc.ca
CWD was confirmed for the first time in B.C. in January 2024. The B.C. CWD Program has implemented a
response plan that is focused on limiting disease transmission and spread to new areas.
Hunters can help by understanding the risks of CWD. Materials that contain CWD prions, such as
carcasses and urine-based scents, can introduce CWD to new areas, contaminate the environment
and expose wildlife. Please follow regulations to reduce the risk of CWD spread by human activity. If
transporting cervid parts from areas affected by CWD be aware of the risks and dispose of this material
in a landfill. Ensure tools and equipment are properly cleaned (40% bleach solution has been effective on
metal surfaces).
Hunters and trappers can also help by submitting samples. CWD testing provides critical information
needed to support science-based disease management. If you hunt deer, elk, or moose, please submit
samples for testing. Submission of samples from harvested deer is mandatory in the CWD Management
Zone in the Kootenay Region. Learn about how and where to submit samples at: www.gov.bc.ca/
chronicwastingdisease.
Jurisdictions neighboring B.C. may have restrictions on the import or transport of cervid carcasses aiming
to reduce potential CWD spread. It is the hunter’s responsibility to be aware of the regulations that apply in
the jurisdiction they are in.

Bird Health
Reports of sick and dead wild birds are of interest to several government agencies and bird enthusiasts. If
you find a dead wild bird – please participate in our BC Interagency Wild Bird Mortality Program. What to
report: 3 or more dead birds in the same geographic location or individual birds of the following species;
species at risk, water-associated birds or raptors. For more information see: www. gov.bc.ca/wildlifehealth
or call 1-866-431-BIRD (2473).
